blocks.x: We're interviewing Anthony Foster again, Chai Ni. Just a second. We're going to get started again. We were going to ask you, Chai Ni, about the way you would blow into a drum. You mentioned how you blow in a drum, sort of sing into it?
Sing and blow it too.
What kind of a tone do you get out of it then?

Well, most of the tone that imitates the song that we'll be playing. Well, I'd take it and I'd blow in the drum there and sometimes imitate a lion or cow, pig, or chicken, or something like that, duck, or anything like that. But it would be on the rhythm that the style that I would be playing on.
Yeah, sure. Do you play a whole chorus like that or just one move?
A whole chorus. Sometimes two, three of them. Because of how long the band, how the band's feeling and what mood they were in.
Now, do you still keep your bass drum going?
Bass drum still goes.
Uh-huh. But you don't use your snare drum?
One hand on the snare drum and the other one with the drum up to my mouth.
Oh, I see. One hand on your snare drum, you say?
One hand on the snare drum and my feet still working, how'd you be playing?
Now, wait a minute. Is it the snare drum you hold to your mouth? It is the snare drum you use?
Yeah, the snare drum to my mouth.
All right. Well, you've got your bass drum going.
The bass drum going.
And you're holding your snare drum up with one hand?
With one hand and beat it with the other hand. And you beat on it? Beat on it with the other hand.
Oh, so you hold it up with your left hand to your mouth?
Get up on it with the left hand to my mouth, just like this.
You might show us how, even if we can't see it on the record.
There you go. I've been playing. I get up from the stool.
Oh, you stand up, yeah.
I hold it down this way.
Oh, yeah, with your left hand.
With the left hand. Uh-huh. And I blow it from the snare side.
Oh, you blow on the skin?
On the skin.
On the skin.
On the skin. With the stick?
With the stick. Oh. And the snare drum never stopped. Oh, but you're blowing on the skin? On the skin. On the snare side? On the snare side. Oh, I thought you were blowing in the wood.
No. Oh, I see. See, you have to blow with the snares and the ears.
Well, in other words, you're letting your lips rattle on the skin?
On the skin and the snare.
Ah, I see.
In other words, anything that I do with my mouth, it'll come out in the drum. Besides the beating of the drum.

It wouldn't work with it on that one skin on the other side? No. No. It wouldn't take it. No, it wouldn't take it. You'd have to have any snares there. I'd have to have a snare. I've seen Sammy Penn sometimes. He holds the drum to his cheek and sing. And that sort of makes it rattle a little.
They covered that from me. Yeah, they got that from you, huh? Yeah. But you hold your lips right up. I hold my lips right up.
Uh-huh.
See, and I tunes the drum. Like I told you once before, you have to tune the drum to that to make those things.
Uh-huh.
You cannot make it just break because it'll sound too much like a mouth.
Yeah, yeah.
This way, it sounds exactly like the rattling of the drum.
Well, do you tune it higher or lower? Yeah, I tune it higher. Yeah. Tune it a minute.
See, and I use my quick snares changes, and I have this hand on that thumb like that. Oh, I see. And I can move my snares up and down.
Uh-huh.
Put it to whatever I'm going to imitate. I push it up or bring it down. Well, for... I'm going to make it higher, bring it up. If I'm going to make it lower, I bring it low.
Well, for instance, for a lion, would you have it lower for a lion?
Lower for a lion.
And what about a chicken or something?
Chicken? I bring it up a little.
Bring it up a little.
Bring it up a little.
Oh, very good. I'd like to hear...
Otherwise, just like I'm going to throw my voice, that's where I guide the snares. Yeah, very good.
So your left hand's holding the drum. Your right hand can operate the snares. Operate the snares. Yeah. And if you don't need the snares, you can still beat on it with the sticks.
Still beat on it with the sticks.
Uh-huh.
But in other words, I'm always using the sticks. Uh-huh.
You'll use your sticks in your hand anyway, whether you operate the snares or not.
That's right. Uh-huh. That's very seldom I have to... Unless I just want to change a very deep change, you know?
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Like if I'm a chain from a car to a chicken, while I have to throw my voice, that's where it's quite natural. Yeah. Uh-huh. I'll make a run on the... Around the drum, so I can move that snares at the same time without stopping.
He did a lot of things at once there.
Well, that's one thing. Punch and I originated then.
Punch Miller?

Punch Miller, yeah. Him and I is the one that originated then. See, because when we were playing with Jack Carey's band, him and I, we would study all kinds of foolishness. We'd go to bed with that, and we'd get in the barroom, and we'd speak about it. That's something that the other father didn't make. Yeah. And so one night, one night, we were sitting in a barroom called Fabolo, so 3rd and Franklin, coming from the National Park.
Oh, yeah.

And so we got there, and they had the whole hand pianos in the barrooms at the time. Uh-huh. So they asked us to play a couple of numbers, the two being half high. I noticed I was reaching to get my drum off of the piano. Uh-huh. So when I was reaching to get my drum off of the piano, half my voice fell in there. And so the partner said, Johnny, why don't you try something on there? Say, see, that's something that we might can make something on. And so, well, in Tiger Rag, when we started to play in Tiger Rag. And since that's the trombone, the trombone would be making, uh, Yeah, Ben, Yeah, Ben, Ben, Ben, Ben. Well, I'd start imitating animals on there. Like that, you understand what I mean? And then we played one of the local locals, the number of liver stable blues.
Oh, yeah.
And that's why we advanced the blow in the drum.
Ah, uh-huh.
That's when we advanced the blow in the drum, man. That's why we got the idea.
But when was that change?
That's, uh, 1919.
Nineteen ninety?
Nineteen ninety.
Yeah, that's a good job.
It originated at 3rd and Franklin, coming from the National Park.
What was that job at the National Park? Playing for the dancing there?
Dancing there.
Uh, they danced on the ground, did they?
On the ground.
Did they ever lay a tarp on the ground?
They played ball in the daytime and danced at night.
Oh, I see. It was at nighttime.
Yeah, at nighttime.
Now, when you say you played with punch band, did you ever, did you play, uh, advertising jobs on the drum?
Advertising job, yeah. Well, all, all jobs are just advertising, especially the color dancers.
Was Jack Carey then, uh, with that same band or not?
Same band.
He was with that band?
He was with the band.
But it was Punchy's band or Jack's band?
No, it was Jack Carey's band.
Jack Carey's band. Yeah.
Uh-huh. And in the later years, well, Punch pulled out from Jack and made his own band.
Well, who else was in that band besides you and Punch and Jack Carey?
Jack Carey was on trombone, myself on drum, Kid Punch on trumpet, Robichaud playing clarinet, Lorenzo Stahl playing banjo, and Lichester Siles playing baseball. It was six pieces.
You say Robichaud on clarinet? Yeah. Which Robichaud was that?
Uh, Walter Robichaud.
Walter Robichaud. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. That sounded like a good band, wasn't it?

Yeah. Well, we were using six pieces. Uh-huh. That was a big band at the time. Uh-huh. We'd take six pieces, they're much more than what they did with a 12-piece band. Uh-huh. Because man was very powerful at the time, and everybody on his own bottom. You see what I mean?
Everybody on his own bottom, right?
Yeah. What does that mean now? Well, every man for his self.
Yeah.

You see, in the line, that's what I tell plenty of people, to my estimation, the jazz, there's no such thing about jazz. Jazz is what you make it. Uh-huh. See, because there's no writing for jazz. There's no music for jazz. Jazz comes out your head. Uh-huh. You never know what you're going to do until you stumble upon it. Uh-huh. In other words, I would call it a gang of mistakes.
Uh-huh.
Gang of mistakes with quick cover. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

See, because a lot of times, at that time, fellas didn't, you'll count the fellas that read music. Uh-huh. A quiet national, a good, uh, fella that's got a good head, loin by air. Well, you hear your reading man play something, a piece that is never heard. But sometimes he'd be hitting at the piece. And make a mistake and he'd make a run on it. And keep making that, and quiet national, that's what you would call jazz. That's what I would call jazz. Gang of mistakes.
Ha-ha-ha. That was pretty good.

Johnny, I wonder if we could take a picture that close up of the way you hold your sticks there. Maybe we can set this drum up. Where did those sticks go? Yeah, is that too high for you? No. You can get a little bit lower if you'd rather. No, that's all right. And let's turn on that other light there, Ralph, will you? And turn that one on over there.
That's exactly the same angle when I'll be playing out of this. Be just about there.
Yeah, if you can move that around anyway, if you like.
Uh-huh.
And I'll try to get up as close as possible.
You want to pull this curtain?
No.
Because you're writing the sum of the camera.
Well, that's all right. Um... Um... It's a minute. I can't get anything there.
Ha-ha-ha-ha-ha-ha. Yeah. You got another one in there?
Yeah, I got this one. Now, what kind of a beater you're doing there, Johnny? That's just an honorary four-four time?

Well, anything you make it, your time, is how you figure it in your head. See, because I can take and make a one beat on the bass drum and still make a four-four beat with my hand. Okay. Or else I can make a one-two beat with my hand and still make a four-four beat on the bass drum. Uh-huh. It's just either in changing the position, changing from your hand to your foot.

Might pull that curtain a little bit, Ralph. All right. And maybe have the sticks down so I can see more of your hands as you're doing it there, yeah. This is going to be too bright. But anyway, I think I can get a good try on that way. You're going to get a slow explosion, huh? Yeah. Yeah. I'll try a fifth of a second. Is there any more light we can get? Well, you can put that one over there. Guess not. That's this one here. All right. Plug this in over there.

Now, Mr. Ralph, you were asking me about two differences in the time. Uh-huh. Well, that's what I was telling you. You see, you don't necessarily, when you're playing a number, a drummer, he makes the time according to his feelings. Now, you see, for instance, I'd be playing a number in a two-four time. You understand?
Uh-huh.

Well, all right. I'll play this way. You see? Now, you notice the dip now switches from my feet to my hand. From my hand back to my feet. All right. But you still have the same tempo as according to the time that the band are playing. All right. So, for instance, we'll be playing a piece in a two-four time. See? Thank you. Thank you. That takes quite a bit of doing to switch around like that, huh? Well, after you know it, it comes in. Now you pay close attention. Now watch. Now watch. Now watch. Now watch.
Now watch. Thank you. Thank you.
Yeah, yeah.
But the going out course is usually sort of a loud one?
Sound and loud and you make all your breaks or something like that.
Do you ever make the first chorus kind of loud too?
Yeah. Yeah. Necessarily. See, because it's quite natural when you fall down in the triode, you're going to play
soft.

You're playing when you fall down in the melody, everybody's going to play soft in order to hear the bass violin and the guitar, banjo, piano, whatever, you use it. And that's when you're going out, everybody for themselves, you're playing in full power. Everybody blasting as loud as they possibly can.
Why is it that you always sort of play loud on the last chorus? Why is that?
Well, that's to swing the people that's dancing. So you give them a great feeling. Uh-huh.
It always seems to me, I don't know, it seems to me that when you play loud on that last chorus, it leaves everybody sort of feeling good about it.
Feeling good, that's right.
Is that the idea?

Yeah. That's to get their mind upset. Get their mind upset. That's right. And when you go in the melody, when you're playing in the melody, and you want to get the harmony out of it, well then you drop down and get a little... Nice and soft, yeah.
Seems like a lot of these bands that play now, they don't seem to do that. They seem to play the same sort of loudness all the way through. All the way through.
Uh-huh.
But that's not right.

No. No, I wouldn't say it was right. No. In other words, because you... ...StługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStług
be sounding like the same thing all the time.
Well that's right. It makes it kind of a contrast when you come down softly and then go out loud again.

In other words, generally when the bass violin and the piano and the banjo, I mean, or either the ghetto, either one that we'd be using, well most of the time, when we fall down in the melody, that's when I was generally using my sticks.
It's a little quieter.

Yeah, the band will settle down. But in order that you hear every band for men. Like a bass player, he'd be thumbing the bass and things like that. But every now and then I may get up off of my drum. Leave my drum and walk over to his bass. He'd be playing the bass and I'd play the drum on the bass while he'd be playing it.
Oh yeah? You play the sticks on the strings then?

On the strings. I leave my drums. You see? Because all the time, all the time when I be, all the time when they're playing down in the harmony part, well my drums is over here. And I walk from over there, I could be playing that just in there, and I walk over to him like that, I'd be playing like that. Oh yeah, but playing the strings. Can I get up to here? When I get there, then he'd be finging the bass and I'd be playing on it.
You have a viol in here, maybe we can demonstrate it on here. Alright, you don't think that would hurt?

It won't hurt it, I don't care if he scratches it. See? Alright, you see I'm walking from the drum. Alright. Walking from the drum towards the bass violin. Then you finger while I play. Now just anything you finger on there, that's what's gonna come out with the stick. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Hey, that's pretty good. somethin' new there.
Hey, that's pretty good.

We invent something new there. You see, we saw all them different stuff like that. If it sounds good, but we'd keep it up like that. We'd meet another band in the street, and we'd get playing at each other, you know, jamming at each other. Well, we'd use those different tactics on them.
Then you think it was about the first time you started hitting on the bass that way.
Yeah.
What band were you with?

With Jack Carroll. Back in Jack Carroll. See, because Jack Carroll was what we called a real ball house band. We would call it a real ball house band. Then in the later years, then they started to call it a jazz. But it was real what you call real old wild, just what you make up your own song.
Yeah, sure.

In other words, the majority of the people would call you a ball house band. Yeah, I don't know. See, because plenty of halls, they wouldn't let us play. They said they didn't want that ball house band. That's because they ain't going to ruin their good people. The characters are their good people. We'd be playing different blues and things like that, just like I'm telling you. Well, Kid Punch was a, not say because I played with him, but Punch is a man that he can hear you play anything. And Punch is going to come right play. If he don't play, he's going to play something just like it. He's going to make some parts in there, or the real stuff, and then he's going to put his parts on it. And then you can't tell if he's doing that on purpose or if he's not, it's an old number.

Well, I was going to ask a couple of questions. Yeah, go ahead. Last time you were telling something about Jones' home, you said you were in the home for a while. For a while. Was that before Armstrong was there?
Before, yeah, before. He was not there when I was there. In other words, they didn't have no band at all.
Didn't have a band even.
Didn't have a band at all. They didn't even have a pair of sticks there.
Yeah.
What they did have, they had an old bugle. Well, they gave us little wooden guns which were drilled like soldiers.
Oh, yeah.
And the boy would blow the bugle.
Remember who was blowing the bugle?
Ike Smoot.
Oh, Ike Smoot.
Ike Smoot.
You mentioned the other day you thought he was better than Armstrong, you said?
Yeah, but he didn't. Before he could make his reputation, he died.
Did he ever play in any jazz bands or dance orchestra work?
Yeah, he played with a band they called the Poylton Band.
Which one?
Poylton.
Poylton.
Yeah.
Do you remember who else was in that?
Well. Were they young kids or older men? No, they were young kids. They were young kids. In other words, that's what they was going to name the band, you see?
Yeah.
Well, just as they got the band organized, he got killed.
Yeah. He got killed? How was that?
Got shot.
Oh, he did? Oh, yeah. Oh. Oh, what, in a fight or something?
Yeah, there was fighting.
Oh.
Yeah. Coming from a dance.
Oh. How long before Armstrong's time were you in that home? A year and a half. A year and a half before Armstrong. Before. Yeah. Well, you left a year and a half before Armstrong went in. Went in.
I see, yeah.
So, there must have been some time in that year and a half that they organized the band.
The band, yeah. Uh-huh. You see, because I had a brother. Uh-huh. Was there, and I used to go there on Sundays and Wednesdays to see my brother.
Uh-huh. Yeah.
Well, about, once, I'd say about a year afterwards, that was they organized the band. Uh-huh. When I'd go there to see my brother, well, I'd go there with the band, practice with the band.
Uh-huh. Now, what did they have? They had all the instruments by that time?
No, they did not have all the instruments.
What did they have?
They had a snare drum. They used a tub for bass drum. Uh-huh. And had a clarinet and two old trumpets. Oh. And a bass horn.
Uh-huh.
Well, that's voice session was a bass horn, you know. Uh, Lewis. That's the song song, voice session was a bass horn.
That same bass horn?
Same bass horn. Back at Jones. His voice session was a bass horn.
Uh-huh. Now, was Rene in the band at that time?
Rene was playing clarinet.
Oh, he was playing clarinet at that time.
Ike, the other boy was Ike Smoop.
And he was on the cornet.
On the cornet. Uh-huh. That little boy about my size named George Washington was playing trombone.
Oh, yeah. I remember hearing about you. George Washington. He played with Buddy Petit. Yeah, Buddy Petit. He's in that picture that's taken.
Uh-huh.
What about Schatz? Was he in the home when you were there? No.
Schatz was not there.
Not then. No. Any other musicians that you can think of in the home at that time or a little later?
Uh. Well, Rene Lice Armstrong. Red Happy. My brother, which is Henry Foster, playing baritone. And, uh, Old Folks. Jim O'Brown.
Who was the other fellow you said, Old?
Jim O'Brown.
Somebody else before that.
Old Folks? Old Folks.
Old Folks.
Is that his name? No, that's the other. That's how we used to call him back there. Yeah.
Yeah. Old Folks. What did he play?

Well, he was smaller than me, so you couldn't imagine. Well, he had a hard-looking face. Oh, yeah. And he never did know his age. Nobody could tell his age because they'd ask him his age. He'd say, I'm so-and-so. Well, who told you that? That's what they told me, so they say. That's all we could get out of him. That's why we called him Old Folks.
What instrument did he play?
Alto.
Alto horn, yeah.

And then, by the way, I'm glad you asked me. There's another boy there. I guess you might have seen him. He was in that band. I'll bring him around sometime. I guess you see him every day, mostly, if you ever hit around Canal Street.
Oh, yeah? Who's that?
He probably got no legs at all. Dog following. He got no legs at all. Right on the little scooter.
Oh. Oh, I've seen the fella.
The dog boy.
I guess I've seen.
Black boy.
He was there at that time?
He was there at that time. He had his two legs.
Oh.
Remember his name? Huh? Remember? Henry Mahoney.
Mahoney.

Henry Mahoney. Oh, huh. He'd be on Canal Street, catching right in front of the Boston Club. Every evening, he'd be out there picking up nickels and dime. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Now, he was a great drummer, too, at one time.
Oh. What happened? Did he have an accident or something?
It canceled.
Oh, canceled.
Canceled, yeah.
Oh, two minutes.
Well, that's where they got the idea of building the band, through him and me.
Yeah.

And we used to take railroad spikes and play on the side of the wall. Oh, yeah? And sometimes we'd take the forks out the kitchen. I'd use the fork, and he'd use the cooking spoon and beat on the tub. I'd beat on the basin. And then, from that on, old man Dave got the idea of building up a band back there.
Oh, I see. Yeah. Uh-huh.
See? So, about that time, my mama got me out to make my communion out to St. Castle Church. That was in the year 1910.
Uh-huh.
First time they brought the band out, when the band got organized, they brought the band out, was 1913.
Yeah.
That's when the band made the police appearance out in the street. Well, they started the band somewhere around between 1912 and 1911.
Uh-huh.
Yeah. In the year, in May, the Hot Pallers had a parade. That's the first time, Jones Band come out. Oh.
Was Louis in the band then?
He was in the band.
And Rene?
Rene, too.
Would Shots be in the band by that time?
Shots was nowhere else around. Uh-huh. Shots was at even playing trumpet.
No.
In other words, if you really want to know, Shots just started playing trumpet around here in 19, uh, around, I'd say around 1922.
Really? I didn't know that late.

Yeah. Yeah. Hmm. Yeah, because, uh, Celestine and Risley, Alepia, Alepia, 1921. And they brand, they band broke up in the latter part of 1921 and 1922. Risley took one part of the Tuxley, the band, and Celestine took one part. Yeah. Well, Shots was just coming out and playing trumpet there. Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Oh, I was going to ask, uh, about that loving cup you mentioned before.
Yeah.
That you won. What was that for? And, uh...
That's what I told you, that, uh, blowing the drum.
You won that at that time?
At that time, yeah. Yeah. Blowing the drums and beating the sticks.
Where was that? I don't think you got all that on tape, though. Was that all? I don't believe it. No. Not the other. Last time, you didn't mention...
You said you still had that loving cup at home.
Yeah, I still have.
I would like to take a photograph, maybe, sometime. Okay. Some time. Yeah. And, uh, where was that that you won that?
Southern Yacht Club.
Were you in competition with any band at that time?
Yeah.
Who were you?
Well, it was, uh, Red Happi was playing drums.
Oh, I see. Oh, that's right.
Red Happi.
And you were with what band?
I was with Celestine.
And Red Happi was with?
Robichaux.
With Robichaux. I see, yeah. Uh-huh. And that was the competition of the Southern Yacht Club.
Yeah, the Southern Yacht Club. Played for Commodore's Rankin.
Ah, I see. And did the band get the loving cup, or just you?
The band got it.
The band got it. Uh-huh.
The band got it.
Okay.

Very good. Well, that was the first loving cup that we got. Uh-huh. So when I got there in the visual loving cup for the drum playing, I had left Punch Band to go with the tuxedo band. Uh-huh. So Black Happi. You see, you had two other Happis.
Yeah.
One is James William, which is Red Happi. And Black Happi is Happy Goldstone.
Uh-oh. What was Red Happi's real name?
James William.
William. I thought it was Bolton or something.
William.
William. I didn't know that.
No, Goldstone. That's Black Happi.
Yeah, Goldstone. Yeah. He's still living. Yeah.
It was just two, two Happis.
Two Happis.
Two Happis. Uh-huh. And Red and Black Happi.
Yeah.
Now, did they both play, I've noticed that Black Happi will play both snares and sometimes bass drums in parades. Did Red do the same thing?
He done the same thing.
Both of them. Either one. Yeah.
He was my hardest competitor.
He was, huh?
Yeah. He was my hardest man. That's the man I fed. Yeah. I'm sorry, I got old. Well, quite nice. So, he was playing a long time before me.
Oh, he was playing before you.
He must have been older than you. He's older. Yeah, he's older. Yeah. Well, after I got up with him, well, I didn't care about nobody else.
Yeah. Yeah.

In other words, in other words, I took his own stuff. Well, I didn't say my own stuff, but the band said it. The first man that gave me the credit was Emil Bigard. Oh, yeah. That man, you're poor race, come along, he heard me. And he said I was a better drummer. Oh, yeah. So, then we come back, they kept bucking against each other out in the street, after we went with me. So, I left the punch band, went with the tuxedo band. So, the night that we was a player up at Salisthans Pavilion, they had a dance at the Italian Hall. To Black Happy, he'll tell you the same thing. He's scared to go up against Red Happy.
Oh, yeah?

So, I told him, if I got the layoff from my job, I'm going to come down there and I'm going to play against Happy. I said, Salisthans for once and all. Well, that's where I got the 11 cup. At the Italian Hall? At the Italian Hall. That's my name between Burgundy and Rampart.
Here's a picture. I took those pictures the other day after you left, about the next day.
Yeah.
That's the Italian Hall there.
That's the Italian Hall, yeah.
And you told us about this other place on Elysian Field.
Elysian Field in Dolphin. That's it, yeah. What went on there? That's the dance up here.
Upstairs?
Upstairs, yeah.
Do you remember any name for that hall?
Lusitano.
Oh, that's Lusitano.
That's the Lusitano Hall.
Who's band did you play with there?
Fishers.
Fishers.
It was Fishers Band and they had Schillings Band, too.
Oh, yeah. They were both white bands?
White bands, yeah. Yeah, they were white bands.
Were there any colored persons in other than, I mean, yourself? I mean, was there any other colored?
No, just me.
Just yourself.
Yeah. In other words, now don't get me wrong. I wasn't a member of the band.
Not a regular member.
No. But they knowed me.
Yeah.

segments.title: Blowing and singing into the drum to imitate animals
segments.summary: Foster explains he sings and blows into the drum, imitating a lion, cow, pig or chicken in rhythm, for a chorus or two.

segments.title: How the snare drum is held and blown on while the bass drum keeps going
segments.summary: Allen presses for the mechanics: he stands, holds the snare drum to his mouth with the left hand, blows on the snare-side skin, and keeps beating with a stick and the bass drum.

segments.title: Tuning the drum and moving the snares to change the animal sound
segments.summary: He tunes the drum higher, shifts the snares by thumb to go lower for a lion or higher for a chicken, and keeps playing with sticks throughout.

segments.chapter: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
segments.title: Origin of blowing the drum with Punch Miller at 3rd and Franklin
segments.summary: He and Punch Miller, in Jack Carey's band, hit on the trick in a barroom on the way from National Park in 1919; the park held dances at night after ballgames.

segments.chapter: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
segments.title: Jack Carey's six-piece band and its personnel
segments.summary: Advertising jobs, Carey's band versus Punch's later band, and the six players including Walter Robichaux on clarinet; six pieces outdid a twelve-piece band.

segments.chapter: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
segments.title: What jazz is: no writing, a gang of mistakes with a quick cover
segments.summary: Foster says jazz is whatever you make it, comes from the head, and is a run of mistakes covered quickly.

segments.chapter: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
segments.title: Setting up the drum for photographs
segments.summary: Russell arranges lights, curtain and drum position to photograph how Foster holds his sticks.

segments.chapter: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
segments.title: Keeping time: switching the beat between hand and foot
segments.summary: Foster demonstrates keeping four-four on the bass drum while the hand plays one-two, and switching between feet and hand in two-four time.

segments.chapter: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
segments.title: Playing soft in the melody and loud on the last chorus
segments.summary: Dropping down on the melody so the bass and banjo are heard, then everyone blasting the out chorus to swing the dancers; modern bands lack the contrast.

segments.chapter: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
segments.title: Playing the drumsticks on the bass violin strings
segments.summary: During quiet passages he leaves his drum and beats the strings of the bass while the player fingers; they demonstrate it and use such tricks against rival bands in the street.

segments.chapter: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
segments.title: Jack Carey's band as a ball house band; Punch Miller's playing
segments.summary: Foster says Carey's band was called a ball house band before the word jazz, some halls refused it, and Punch could copy or embellish anything.

segments.title: Foster's time in the Jones Home before Armstrong; bugle and Ike Smoot
segments.summary: The home had no band then, only a bugle played by Ike Smoot, who was killed after a dance before his band formed; Foster left about eighteen months before Armstrong arrived.

segments.title: The home's first band and its instruments
segments.summary: Visiting his brother, Foster practiced with the new band: snare, tub bass drum, clarinet, two trumpets, bass horn; Rene on clarinet, Smoot on cornet, George Washington on trombone.

segments.title: Other boys in the home: Old Folks, Henry Mahoney, his brother Henry
segments.summary: Foster names musicians at the home including Red Happy, his brother Henry on baritone, Old Folks on alto, and Henry Mahoney, later a legless Canal Street beggar who had been a fine drummer.

segments.title: How the home band got started; first parade in 1913
segments.summary: He and Mahoney played on spikes, forks and tubs, which gave the bandmaster the idea; his communion was 1910 and the band first paraded in 1913.

segments.title: When Louis, Rene and Kid Shots joined; the Celestin and Ridgley split
segments.summary: Armstrong and Rene were in the band by its first parade; Shots only began trumpet around 1922 when Ridgley and Celestin's bands broke up.

segments.title: The loving cup won at the Southern Yacht Club
segments.summary: Foster describes the loving cup for drum blowing won with Celestin's band in competition with Robichaux's band, with Red Happy on drums.

segments.title: Rivalry with Red Happy and Black Happy; the cup at the Italian Hall
segments.summary: Foster distinguishes the two Happys, calls Red his hardest competitor, recalls Emile Bigard's praise, and a contest against Red at the Italian Hall after he left Punch's band for the Tuxedo band.

segments.title: Lusitano Hall and playing with white bands as the only Black boy
segments.summary: Photos of the Italian Hall and the Lusitano Hall on Elysian Fields; he sat in with Fischer's and Schilling's white bands though not a regular member.

segments.title: The Masonic hall on Dolphin Street and other dance halls
segments.summary: Russell and Foster sort out a hall on Dolphin Street, once white and now Black, versus one at Mandeville and Rampart.

segments.title: The old schoolhouse hall at Touro and Dolphin; halls burned and rebuilt
segments.summary: A former schoolhouse with dancing downstairs burned twice and was rebuilt; Foster first played the Mandeville and Rampart hall with Chris Kelly, and a white hall is mentioned.
